28. The testimony above though asserting that Vanu's death was not self-inflicted arrives at that point circuitously by various assertions and opinions that do not unequivocally substantiate that conclusion or invariably lead to it. Rather, the doctor's testimony in cross-examination is equivocal in its drift and suggestive of the possibility of the bruises being consequential to suicidal hanging and, therefore, cannot be relied upon solely and exclusively to corroborate the prosecution case of homicide. In this regard, this Court finds that the ratio decidential. of the judgment in Abul Hossain Khan vs State reported in 8 BLC (AD) 172 cited by the learned Deputy Attorney General M Bhishmadev Chakrabortty and as attaches weight and significance to a doctor's expert opinion pursuant to the provisions of sections 45 of the Evidence Act, 1872 much of its significance in the present scenario. The learned DAG has further relied on the judgment in Ilias Hussain vs State reported in 54 DLR (AD) 78 recognizing the husband's duty to explain the circumstances of his wife's death occurring while in his custody and the adverse presumption that is attendant upon any failure to so duly discharge the duty by reason of his absconsion. The Ilias Hussain Case is also authority for a natural presumption to arise in such circumstances of the commission of murder by the husband which read with the ratio decidendi in Joynal Bhuiyan vs State reported in 52 DLR 179 subjects him to the natural expectation of the law to explain the cause of his wife's death. Any failure to fulfil such expectation, as held in State vs Md Eraj Meah reported in 9 BLC 570 would, in all likelihood, lead to the irresistible conclusion as to the husband's guilt. 

 29. It is in this regard that this Court finds merit in Mr Amir-ul-Islam's argument in response that even before this Court can identify absconsion as fortifying of guilt the necessary precondition is of a preponderance of evidence pointing to murder. However, there being no preponderous evidence in this case for the assignation of guilt beyond a shadow of doubt, the resort to such presumption predicated overwhelmingly on that fact of absconsion, in the view of this Court, would undeniably lead to a serious miscarriage of justice. Here this Court finds it prudent to subscribe to the pertinent judicial reasoning that even an innocent person, upon implication for a serious crime, might be compelled to abscond to avoid harassment and the corollary view that absconsion per se is not be treated as an incriminating condition (State vs Lalu Miah reported in 39 DLR (AD) 117). That dictate reminds this Court of the primary, therefore, to be accorded to the particular facts of a given case as the primary determinant of deducing whether absconsion is due to any guilty knowledge or to any intention to avoid police harassment or some such other innocuous reason. This Court, in the facts and circumstances therefore, finds substance in Mr Islam's submissions that the condemned-prisoner in all probability, and for want of any credible evidence to the contrary, escaped from the spot in fear of harassment but without any guilty mind and that in that context mere absconsion without any guilty mind cannot be an overriding basis for conviction. The case against absconsion being a determinant of guilt becomes even more compelling in a case as this where the where the other circumstances of the prosecution case are not satisfactorily established (Shahjahan vs State reported in. It is here that this Court finds that the Tribunal, from the facts and circumstances before it, and notwithstanding its express dissatisfaction with the investigation process, veered towards finding on murder without satisfaction that the prosecution has proved its case beyond all reasonable doubt. And it is precisely here that the Tribunal seriously erred in law by failing to discharge its duty to adequately scrutinize this case and resorting to according undue reliance upon analogical deduction.
